what_it_does: Federated learning (also called collaborative learning, or CL) trains AI models by sending the work to users' phones and laptops instead of copying their data to a server — but in practice dozens of different training jobs compete for the same limited pool of devices that are only available when charging on Wi-Fi. Today's systems assign devices to jobs randomly, which wastes scarce devices and makes every job take much longer. Venn is a smarter scheduler that understands which jobs are competing for the same rare devices and prioritizes accordingly, cutting average job completion time by up to 1.88x.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Each CL job specifies requirements — for example, 'I need a device with at least 4 GB of RAM' — and needs hundreds or thousands of participating devices per training round. When multiple jobs run at once, their eligible device pools may overlap (two jobs both want high-memory phones), be nested (one job accepts any phone, another accepts only premium ones), or be completely separate. Random matching ignores these relationships entirely: it may give the scarce premium-phone slots to a job that would have been fine with any device, while the job that specifically needs premium phones waits. Venn models this as what it calls the Intersection Resource Scheduling problem.

How it works. Venn has two algorithms.

Scheduling algorithm (minimizing waiting time): Jobs are first grouped by what kind of device they need — all jobs requiring the same hardware spec go into one group. Within each group, jobs are sorted by shortest remaining demand first (a job that needs 10 more devices gets served before one that needs 500). Then across groups, Venn must decide how to allocate devices that could go to multiple groups. The rule: look at the ratio of queue length to allocated devices for each group. The group with the higher ratio (many jobs waiting, few devices allocated) gets priority on the contested devices. This greedy allocation runs in time proportional to the number of jobs times log(jobs) plus the square of the number of device groups — fast enough to run at scale.

Matching algorithm (minimizing response time): Once a job is scheduled, there is a secondary problem: the slowest-responding device in a round determines when the round ends. Venn partitions devices into tiers by hardware capability and randomly assigns one tier per job round (not always the fastest tier, to ensure diversity of device experience). It only activates this tier-based selection when the math shows it will actually reduce total job time — specifically, when the response-time speedup from using a homogeneous fast tier outweighs the extra waiting needed to accumulate that tier's devices.

The key design choice. Decoupling the two problems (who gets served first vs. which devices they get) keeps the algorithm tractable. Triage by group scarcity catches the most important inefficiency — wasting a rare device type on a job that does not need it — without solving a computationally intractable matching problem.

Fairness safeguard. Because the shortest-first rule can starve large jobs indefinitely, Venn includes a fairness knob (a parameter from 0 to 1) that adjusts job priority based on how far each job has fallen behind its fair-share completion time. Setting the knob higher trades some average-speed improvement for guarantees that no job waits too long.

The result. Compared to the random matching used by Apple, Meta, and Google's production CL systems: up to 1.88x faster average job completion time across five real-world workload types. Jobs competing for the rarest device types see the biggest gains — up to 8.7x faster in the most resource-constrained scenarios.
